utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic and Vladimir Santic also know as "Vlado".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. President, just a short announcement on the order of witnesses for today. We've already informed Defence counsel that we'll be putting witness number 6 on first before witness number 5 because of witness number 6's obligations to be elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Of course, we are sorry about this short delay, and there may be problems at the detention unit, but I will send a note to the commanding officer so that in future we will not have to wait. We thought we should start with the proceedings without the accused, because we might take about five to ten minutes to discuss procedural matters. There are two points in particular. One point, which is of some importance, is we have now decided to go to Ahmici on the 20th of October, which is a Tuesday, to visit Ahmici on Tuesday the 20th of October. And we have to draw up a sort of itinerary, and for this we need the submissions of Defence counsel other than Counsel Krajina. I wonder whether those commissions are ready, because we would need them today so we can take them into account while making those plans. I was also wondering whether we could have, from either party or both parties, some sort of rough indication about Ahmici. I was thinking there should probably be a short history of Ahmici, and what is even more important is the social composition of this village, say, the level of education and the sort of jobs, I mean, the occupation of inhabitants, whether they were farmers, what sort of job they had, whether they were working -- I mean, a rough idea. I am aware that this is very difficult to have a breakdown of statistics, but it might be helpful also to have an idea of the social background and also the history of this village. This was my first problem. The second matter is about the Witness SA, the lady, you remember. We have now decided to call this witness as a court witness, and we would like to seek your views about how to go about the matter. I mean, the examination of this particular witness. We would be inclined to suggest that we Judges would start off by putting questions to this witness, and then she could be cross-examined by Defence counsel and re-examined by the Prosecutor. I think this will be in the interests of justice and also would be appropriate. Of course, she would have to be -- how shall I say -- protected by the unit, and the unit should be in charge of this witness when she comes here, and should also explain how things go on in court, because I'm sure that she does not know how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Yes. In fact, this witness will be called in conformity with Rule 98 of this Tribunal, so this witness is no longer a Prosecution witness as had been the case until then. This witness has not been proved by the Prosecution, so I do think that indeed Your Honours should be the first ones to question this witness, and then I think that the Prosecution should be entitled to examine the witness and then the Defence counsels could question her. I think that this order is the one which should be respected, Your Honours, the Prosecution and then the Defence. But maybe this is a personal view that you do not share.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But you agree, of course, with the fact that the witness should be protected by the Victim and Witnesses Unit, and I myself favour the view that a representative of the Victim and Witnesses Unit should be present in the courtroom to give her a psychological support.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But then you think that the Judges should begin first and then the Prosecution and then the Defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: That is quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So let us turn towards the Defence counsel to see what they think of your proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. As far as the question of calling and hearing the witnesses -- the witness, I think that the Defence counsel of Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic could say a few words on that, because we're dealing with a witness testifying to facts which they are interested in. As far as your request is concerned, that is that you -- we give you some background information, that is for the Trial Chamber, on Ahmici, the Defence counsel will look into the matter and perhaps in the course of the day we'll inform you of that matter. We're going to ask somebody to prepare information of that kind for the Trial Chamber, and we're then going to give you an answer in the course of the day. I don't know if there are any other matters that you mentioned. At the same time, I would like to apologise, when discussing preparations for the trip and everything that should be looked at during the trip, it is true that our colleague Mr. Krajina did not think about the matter but Defence counsel has different views on this issue. Some of them think that they have nothing to draw your attention to specifically because it does not stem from their Defence cases, whereas the others think that this would be disclosure of strategy, Defence strategy or Defence tactics, but at any rate, we'll be informing you in due course, perhaps after the first break, of how things stand and the stand of Defence counsel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Of course, we are not asking you to make submissions about the trip. If you prefer not to submit anything, you are free to do so. It's just because the Defence Counsel Krajina made submissions, we thought that other Defence counsel might also wish to propose to the court particular items to be seen and so on. But you are free to refrain from submitting anything. As to the background information, you don't need to rush. You can give us this background information in one week or ten days. In any case, before we go there. Thank you. Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: As my colleague Mr. Pavkovic has said that Defence counsel for the brothers Kupreskic will be saying a few words, and my colleague Mrs. Glumac and myself have different standpoints, we would like you to decide. I do agree with the proposal made by the Prosecutor that the Defence be last in questioning the witness, because that is in keeping with the legal system which we come from, whereas my learned colleague Mrs. Glumac feels that there should be -- that we should question the witness before the Prosecutor. So we're in your hands completely, and we shall abide by your ruling. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I may be wrong. I thought that Counsel Slokovic-Glumac was not going to set out her views. So do you want to say a few words about this particular point, who should examine this witness first, you or the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I think that we are in a position, and as this is not our witness or the witness of the accused, this is a court witness and as he was called, so after the introductory questions by the Trial Chamber, according to regular procedure, we shall take part in the cross-examination and then the Prosecutor will be interviewing the witness, but my colleague Mr. Radovic thinks that it should be otherwise. So it will be according to your ruling. That is to say we -- our role comes up in cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Our ruling is as follows: There will be, first, questions from the court, then the Prosecutor, then Defence counsel. And we will make plans, that when she comes she can be heard in court the next day so that she doesn't need to stay here too long, because this is to be, for her, quite stressing. All right. We can now bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could I raise something about the on-site visit, which is the actual conduct of the visit. Is anybody going to speak during the visit? Are matters going to be pointed out to the Trial Chamber or not? There are obvious advantages in not having anything said, but there may be difficulties if people want to point something out. I would be grateful if the parties would give some consideration to that. It must be done in an orderly fashion. (The accused entered court) (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: We shall indicate some of the elements which we should like you to see, and in that sense we shall partially be disclosing our Defence tactics, but as we're doing this after the Prosecution has finished presenting his evidence, then it is not important whether we're going to disclose part of our tactics at that particular time or in the introduction. The essential part of our Defence tactics will be made known to you when we show you what we feel you should see. Thank you. And we'll write it down, of course. You'll have it in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to answer Judge May's question. The Prosecution yesterday handed over to the Court a description of Ahmici, and in particular, a description of the sites in Ahmici which the Prosecution thinks are a good thing for you to visit. I think it would be a good thing that during this visit the representatives, both of the Defence and the Prosecution, make a certain number of observations to Your Honours. I think it is useful, and I don't think it poses any problems insofar as the Chamber is perfectly capable, to make the adversarial principle be respected. Of course, if observations are made they will be heard by the other party, and the other party can answer these observations if they don't share what is said. The accused will not be present, that is a fact. That is something that we have thought about. Nonetheless, we think that the adversarial principle will be respected if both the Defence and Prosecution are represented in Ahmici. So I don't think there's any difficulty in that particular situation. You will be able to hear both what the Defence and the Prosecution has to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Let me just add, as a footnote, that we have already made provision for having both audio and video recording of the whole visit so that there will be a record. In addition, minutes will be taken by an official of the registry. So everything will be on paper and video recording. Mr. Moskowitz?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I wonder if -- Your Honours, if it is clear, at this point, from SFOR the kind of access that the Court and counsel will, in fact, have to visit various areas in Ahmici. On the several occasions that I was there, I found my access quite limited by SFOR in where I could go, and I don't know if that sort of attitude has changed with SFOR or whether we'll have more access. And that may, I think, inform the Court as to what the best way would be to converse with counsel. And, of course, I do agree with Judge May that there could very well be difficulties in communication and in drawing attention of the Tribunal to certain things and then other counsel not being present to listen and to make comments. It might be useful to think about limiting contact or conversation to questions that the Tribunal has specifically to ask to counsel rather than to encourage counsel to point to the Tribunal, "Look here, look there." I think it might be a bit of a problem, and that I think the Tribunal should be in total control of the on-site visit and to make the decision as to when and how it should communicate with Defence and Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. As for SFOR, let me tell you that I gather that SFOR is waiting for our itinerary, and in light of our suggestions will decide whether or not we may have access to particular areas. Good. Let us move on. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac, would you like to continue with the cross-examination of the witness? Cross-examined by Ms. Slokovic-Glumac (continued):

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness Y. We have received the marked maps with the plan of defence that we saw yesterday. I'm now going to give you the map with the house numbers, and for the record, could you tell us where the line went in relationship to the houses that are marked on the map and are denoted with a number? I don't think you need draw it in. You could just dictate it to us according to the numbers on the map. I think that would be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: He will have to take the original exhibit then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you explain to me what you actually want me to do once more?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The lines that you made, the defence lines which were positioned, and you said that you had agreed upon them on the 15th, and you drew them on to the map, referring to Ahmici, upper, middle and lower, and Pirici. So tell us, please, beside which houses, looking at the numbers on the map, the numbers denoting the houses, where these lines passed in relation to the houses on the map. They're marked by numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm afraid we can't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You need the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Twenty-one, 22, 23, 26, 27. There are no houses further on, so there are no numbers either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Up to 31 you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere here, exactly here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Above number 33?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thirty-one, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that is the line in Lower Ahmici. What about in middle Ahmici in relation to the houses once again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Seventy-one, 70, 69, 67, 64, 63, 62. I think that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And now for Upper Ahmici, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now for Pirici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two hundred fifty-nine, 258, 255, 254, 251, 250.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, whether the situation in 1993 was such that people in the village were engaged as soldiers of the BH army, and this would stem from your testimony -- that's why I'm asking you -- or whether they were in the guard units, that is to say, that they had some tasks joined to the army in the village, and I'm talking about the military-able men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The able-bodied men had obligations along the frontlines towards the Serbs, and that was the members of the 325th brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did they have an obligation, and where did they perform this obligation on the line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did exist, but on the line, frontline, towards the Serbs exclusively.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that means they were mobilised; can we say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A part of them were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, whether you know that a general mobilisation was proclaimed in Bosnia-Herzegovina by the President of the presidency, Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether this was in a particular period or, if you don't know, did you hear about any lists, population lists, concerning mobilisation being drawn up? You worked in the command, so you must have known about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that, but I do know that we worked on this with the aim of forming a brigade. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any lists of the former Territorial Defence units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why didn't you have these lists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because all the papers had remained in Vitez with the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in Vitez, you did not have a municipal command post of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where Sefkija Dzidic was the commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was formed later on, but at that time, the municipal command in 1992, I don't quite remember whether it was '93 as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because many witnesses have testified to the fact that the Territorial Defence was wholly taken over by the Bosniaks, and that after that, the BH army was established, and that all the records and lists had remained with the Bosnians.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I don't think they remained in the hands of the Bosnians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know when the BH army began to be set up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but I do know that the Patriotic League and the development of the army through the Patriotic League and Territorial Defence, and later on it became an army, but I don't recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What year would that be? What year was the Patriotic League set up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1991, '92, I don't know exactly. I don't know about the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the BH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The BH army I think was set up at the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993, that is its initial, the first steps towards forming the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: We're going to refer to the orders related to the general mobilisation. I should therefore like the usher to take copies of the order, and I would like to ask the witness to have a look at this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D12-2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, in view of the fact that during 1992, at the end of '92 and the beginning of '93, until the conflict in Ahmici, you worked on the formation of the 325th brigade, are you familiar with the information provided in this order, because this served as legal grounds for you for calling up people and asking them to join the BH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I didn't work on this, I only helped people who were working and who were in charge of these papers, and this is the first time I have seen these orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't even know the general mobilisation was declared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't know about that, so how did you -- how did you muster these people? Not everyone was a volunteer, I imagine, so on what basis did you call them up? There is an obligation, during general mobilisation, to accept call-up papers and to respond; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you must have known what the legal grounds for this were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I repeat, I only helped these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you said that you were working in the command. In the village you were helping and over there you were helping too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could these contents be controversial or are you simply unfamiliar with this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not familiar with this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, when the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was established, do you know which corps were formed, and this broader Vitez area, Vitez-Busovaca-Zenica, this region, where did it belong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that our brigade belonged to the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many corps were set up; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Four, I think. I think four were set up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the 3rd Corps covered which area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it include the Zenica area; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I kindly ask the usher to hand in these papers too. This is the decision to set up the corps of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and on the establishment of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D13-2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what about the information provided there; is it correct to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am familiar with the corps that are mentioned here, and these zones of responsibility, that I don't know about. I just know that our brigade belonged to the 3rd Corps. And the 3rd Corps, which zone of responsibility it had, that I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The decision on the establishment of corps of the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, you are not denying this date that is here, that is also the establishment of the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, in view of the fact -- or, rather, let us go back to your work again. You worked at the command, on these lists of men. Do you know what happened to people who came to the Vitez area as refugees? Were they included and in which way were they included or, rather, were they mobilised? Were they sent to certain units? Were they supposed to report to Territorial Defence headquarters? The command? Where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think they were supposed to do so; that is to say, according to the territorial principle, according to where they were staying, in which parts of the village. They simply came in and reported to these units in the command of the brigade, part of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If they stayed there, were they supposed to stay on longer, if they got a house? Was this an obligation that they took upon themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. People would simply stay where there was enough room, where there was enough space, where they were accepted by local people, so there were no obligations involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were records kept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, to the extent possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any problems and were additional papers presented in this period at the end of 1992 and 1993? If a military-age man wanted to leave Bosnia and Herzegovina, did he have to get special permits from the authorities in charge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. No. I don't know. I think that at that time, if people wanted to leave the country, I don't think they reported it to someone, they would simply take care of their papers and leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Ahmici, there were families where the wife and the children would leave and the husbands would stay behind. These were refugees. However, they couldn't get all the right papers. Do you know anything about that? Were they stopped in a way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted). Yesterday you said that that house had a very strong basement and that therefore it was envisaged as some kind of improvised shelter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was in a small ravine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, was there an evacuation plan for civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me say one thing. There were no plans. It was only that we had agreed amongst ourselves. But plans, in the sense of military plans, real plans, they did not exist. So it is only that we agreed amongst ourselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also tell me, since at that time there was civilian defence too and it was involved in various matters and it was partly involved in the implementation of evacuation and even planning of evacuation, do you know whether, through the civilian defence in the Vitez municipality, evacuation plans were made for some villages that could be jeopardised, for example, the village of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person called Fuad Zeco?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know which post he held in 1992, 1993, in addition to being employed as a veterinarian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I don't know. I only know him as a vet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a kind of commander of civilian defence units? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what he did. I think he did work in the civilian defence, but what he exactly did there, I don't know. But could I clarify this a bit further? He worked on civilian defence matters, and this civilian defence, which was attached to the brigade, it was supposed to go and help the army up at the frontline, you see?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They didn't do things related to working out evacuation plans?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many people were involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I checked the transcript, and certain names were not included, so I wish to ask you about this again. These are persons who we mentioned as soldiers under the command of a squad leader. I don't need this. It is the text in the diary of the 14th of March, and this person was elected squad leader and his soldiers are the following persons from the village. First of all, a person called Nasko. Is that Nasid Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The person called Lato, is that Latif Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Huso? Do you know who that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are several Husos and also there are two Latif Ahmics.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters couldn't hear Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a Huso in the middle part of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know his last name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was Krdzalic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Hazro? Hazrudin Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Osman? Was it maybe Budo Osmancevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Alaga?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Alaga is not from that part of the village, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Alaga Ahmic, he is from the lower part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he's from the lower part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it possible that he is that Alaga?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Muamera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what Muamera you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could it be Muamera Pjanic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER

utterances.text: And the people I mentioned to you just now, are most of them military-aged men, the right age to be soldiers?

utterances.text: You said that rather as -- that you started setting up these village guards in 1993 and that you didn't know what was happening in 1992. Do you know anything about the establishment of the Territorial Defence and its development in that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing special. I already said that I was in this mixed unit, so I was only involved in that job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And already in April 1992, already at that time, were certain lists being made in villages? Were some kind of units being set up at that time? This was a year before the attack. Was this at least on paper? Were any records made? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

These were notes that were taken in passing. It is not very well charted, but you can see what it's all about, and you will also see its number in terms of it being admitted as evidence in the Blaskic trial.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D40/2.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to put a few questions, but identity could be revealed directly. So I appreciate it if we could move into closed session, or perhaps we could take a break at this point and continue after the break in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness, I will ask the Prosecutor when they think we will receive the list of witnesses for the next week. Friday or tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning, Captain Woolley. Could you please stand and make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President, because you have already moved on, but we would kindly request the following: We have been informed that tomorrow and the day after tomorrow are not working days, so could the Prosecutor please provide us with a list so that the Defence could prepare itself for these witnesses that are to be heard next week. Why not today rather than on Friday? Why not provide a list of witnesses earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: In response to that, we are still evaluating which witnesses are going to be called and when, and we will provide it, if possible, tomorrow. I think today it is probably not going to be possible because we still haven't finalised our list for next week. Part of the problem is that this last witness went on quite a bit longer than we anticipated and we have other witnesses who are here and then other witnesses who have obligations, so we are trying to balance things out. We will meet today after court to try to finalise that list, and hopefully by tomorrow we will have a list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Tomorrow morning, could you try to provide it --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: We will try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Tomorrow. By the way, you know that we have now two more weeks, even less.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: This is also part of our thinking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. And don't forget that next week, we intend to call the lady, the witness, we mentioned before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: This will be next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Next week, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do we know which day or what day at this point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. We will see -- I hope that by tomorrow both Defence counsel and the Court will receive this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Smith:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major Woolley, you've just recently been promoted, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since making this statement you were, in fact, a Captain but in the last few months have been promoted to Major?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court your occupation at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: I'm a Major in Her Majesty's armed forces in Britain. I'm squadron leader of a reconnaissance Squadron of the 9th/12th Royal Lancers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you join the British army?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: In July 1987.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in November 1992 did you attend in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I was deployed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the purpose for going to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: It was for providing humanitarian aid to beleaguered people within Bosnia as part of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you based?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Throughout most of the time in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long was your tour in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Six months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And prior to going to Bosnia can you give the Court an idea of any other field operations that you've been involved in?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: I served with the United Nations in Cyprus in 1990. I was called back from there to go to the Gulf in 1991, and then I was deployed to Bosnia in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Court the training that you received in relation to being an officer in the British army?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: I spent a year at the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst. Of course, that's general training. And prior to going to Bosnia, received a couple of months of training. And each year we conduct army training directives which include things such as first-aid and the law of armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived in Bosnia, and more specifically at about March/April 1993, can you explain to the Court the general military situation in the Vitez area, the Vitez opstina, and the ethnic origins of the people who lived in that municipality and nearby?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: The ethnic origins of the people of the Vitez opstina were pretty much 50 per cent Croat and 50 per cent Muslim. When we arrived in November'92, the two ethnic groupings, I think socially and militarily, were pretty much in loose alliance. Their common aggressor was the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the particular names of the military groupings that related to the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: The Croat army was known as the HVO or the HVO (pronounced phonetically), and the Muslims as the Bosnian armija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In terms of the Vitez municipality and nearby, can you explain to the Court where any confrontation lines may have been with the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: In that area, the Bosnian Serb frontline was pretty much to the north-west of Vitez in an area called Turbe, just north-west of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court whether there was any presence at all of Bosnian Serb military forces within the municipality of Vitez or the immediate area outside of that?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: No, there weren't. No, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In April you attended a village called Ahmici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you been familiar with that village prior to attending there?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: I'd driven past it but was unaware, like so many of the other small villages around there, that it was just another village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what the predominant population was in relation to ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Predominantly Muslim, quite clearly. And a minaret stands -- or stood very prominent in the front part of the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the general situation in the Vitez municipality in April 1993 before you attended Ahmici, can you explain to the Court what that situation was in military terms?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: As a military -- as a young man, as a young military commander, I wasn't quite as aware of the broad nature of what is going on in that there was not so many significant examples that I was aware of that showed a Muslim-Croat or Croat-Muslim aggression. They seemed to be fairly in loose alliance. But on the night of the 15th there were tangible -- there was tangible evidence that clearly there was a Croat aggression starting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court where you went to on the night of the 15th and what facts have enabled you to come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: I was asked by my company commander to go to a rendezvous point at a junction just short of a village called Putis, which is just slightly beyond the Busovaca junction. And I met him there with a Muslim commander from Zenica, and we entered the village of Putis because we had heard that there was some HVO in the area. We drove up into the village and there was a series of firings -- firing taking place over our heads until we got into the village. It then stopped, and we then saw, through our night sights, soldiers in the woodland, which we had our own guns trained on, but they'd stopped firing so we were unable to take any action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was possible for you to identify who, in fact, these soldiers were that were firing towards you?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: No, not at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were in the village with a Muslim military commander; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that area, the village of Putis, anywhere near a Serb frontline or stronghold?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: No. No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is that what led you to your conclusion that it was from the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Yes. I understood the village to be, from charts, demographic charts in our operations room, that this was a Muslim -- predominantly Muslim village, and, therefore, it would be unusual for Muslims to be shooting at themselves or their families or friends.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from this incident of the shooting, was there anything else significant in that village in relation to damage, or destruction or --

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Not at that time, no. Not at that early stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you -- how did that situation resolve itself with the Muslim commander?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Our presence seemed to create a stalemate, and, therefore, we withdrew. It was night and it was difficult, obviously, to see, and, therefore, we withdrew and recorded the incident as it happened and left it at that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what happened on the morning of the 16th of April? Was there anything of significance that you heard of whilst you were at the Vitez base that morning?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: I had got up, and I was sitting in the officer's mess waiting to be tasked as part of the A Company 1 Cheshire, the battle group company that was on duty. And as I had been attached to the Cheshires, I had a different type of vehicle, I had a Scimitar vehicle, which is a lot less armoured than the Warriors which the Cheshires use, and, therefore, had been instructed not to go into town where there were reports -- I say "town" meaning Vitez -- there were reports there that an action or some sort of aggression was taking place with regard Croat and Muslim. Therefore, I sat in the mess unable to go out, rather frustrated. And a friend of mine, colleague, a commander from the Cheshires, came back from Vitez telling us that the area was generally a battle zone, a lot of civilians and soldiers dead in the streets, houses burning, explosions, gunfire. Generally an unsavoury situation taking place in Vitez and the surrounding areas of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this morning stick out in your mind quite significantly compared to the rest of our tour?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Absolutely and very vividly. Up until that point, the local area had pretty much been in some sort of -- well, there was nothing significant that stood out in that area up until this point. And the morning of the 16th, with the background of the night of the 15th, there had seemed to be this sort of explosion of activity between the Croats and the Muslims that previously had not been there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You heard reports from a colleague of yours as to what was occurring in Vitez. Did you subsequently leave the base and go to the village of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: It was not long after he told me about this that I was then called to the operations room by the Operations Officer of the Cheshire battle group, and tasked to go to a small village called Ahmici, because they understood that there was some action or activity going on there that needed to be investigated and reported upon, and, therefore, I was dispatched down to the village with two of my Scimitars and one Warrior, with an interpreter, a photographer and two Irish ranger soldiers on board.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you briefly explain to the Court the difference between a Scimitar vehicle and a Warrior vehicle and what they're used for?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: A Scimitar vehicle is an 8 tonne light aluminium vehicle, with three crew stations, which is obviously used for reconnaissance, whereas a Warrior is a 35 tonne, very heavily built infantry fighting vehicle that can take three crew stations but also seven infantry men in the back. They have the same guns however.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe the situation as you drove towards the village of Ahmici, what was happening on the way, and when you received your first impressions of what was occurring or what had occurred in the village of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: From deploying from the base of Vitez and taking the ring road around the edge of Vitez through to Dubravica, it was quite clear from looking at the general landscape that there was a series of plumes and pillars of smoke coming from areas, group of houses, none that I can specify, and also outlying villages, and general battle noise, explosions and gunfire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to show you now a copy of an aerial photograph which is, in fact, a reduced copy of the large photograph behind you which has been marked, and if you can explain to the Court where, in fact, you got your first impressions of what was occurring in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be marked Exhibit 229.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major Woolley, is that area familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It's pretty much the area of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can see on that exhibit, so that's Exhibit P229, you can see on that exhibit there is a number of markings. Did you provide the information that led to those markings being placed on the exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you can briefly explain to the Court what the Roman numerals mean in terms of chronology?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: From I to VI they signify significant places, buildings and situations that I conducted -- where I had conducted various actions throughout the day, basically regarding first-aid of injured civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on the day of the 16th of April, you attended the village on one occasion, and then did you attend there on a second occasion or near to it?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: I attended the village in the morning for about four hours, and then in the evening I was on the main road of the village, in this area here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in relation to the duration of your first visit, can you till the Court which points relate to your first visit?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Point I here -- do you want me to explain it in detail?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not in detail, but just the points that relate to --

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Point I is a house where I got involved with a casualty. Point II is a place where I stopped and observed some soldiers. Point III is a house where I dealt with another casualty. Point IV is a place where I dealt with five casualties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the court Point VI?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Point VI is a place just off the main road where I recovered five bodies, with the assistance of another Lieutenant, in the evening of the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Points A and B relate to?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: A and B are two houses which, at about 3.00 on the 16th, were very clearly and freshly on fire, two civilian houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can go back to the time that you first approached the village. From about what location on that map did you obtain your first impression of what was occurring or what had occurred?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: This road here is the road from Vitez, and this road bends round into a small river or ravine. It was on this high ground here that I, at first, identified, from looking at my map relating to the ground, that this was the village of Ahmici. And looking over to my left, I could see that it was a village that had plumes of smoke rising from it, and, therefore, obviously had been in some kind of activity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I ask you to mark that location with a red texter that's in front of you, with an X?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: (Marks).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anything further you can state to the Court that will help them understand your first impressions? You mentioned plumes of smoke rising from houses.

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Yes. As I approached the turnoff to the village -- sorry, the turn into the village, generally speaking there was -- the area was deserted. There was sporadic gunfire, the odd explosion, houses alight and mainly smoking, which generally told me that there had been some sort of destruction, whether military or not, and I was unaware at this point, but probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at about what time did you obtain your first impression? What time did you arrive in the village?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: It was about 11.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your view as to what was occurring or what had occurred? What was the impression that you got?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: I did not adopt an impression until I actually -- I was under the impression that there had been some action and some destruction, but I didn't adopt a particular impression with regard to any ethnic grouping until I spoke to a woman in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said the village was deserted when you arrived. Can you explain how this woman approached you when you first arrived in the village?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: As I approached the village along this small track, or actually driving through the village or the first part of the village. I got to this point here on the track, and had my three vehicles, and I had a woman and a couple of people behind her beckon -- particularly the woman, beckon me from behind -- or, shall I say, from the archway of her door to come and speak to her. She was reluctant to take -- to remove herself from the cover that the door provided her. Therefore, because I was unaware of what she was trying to tell me, I took the prudent measure of going to talk to her in case it was an ambush or a mine up ahead that I was unaware of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the house that she came from was the house marked with the circle with the 14 next to it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the house near the lower mosque?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at these two exhibits that I produced to you now, P81 and P79, I ask they be produced to him. Can you tell the Court who, in fact, is in those exhibits? I think that may be the wrong exhibit. P79 and P81. If you can look at Exhibit P81. You mentioned that this woman beckoned you and you attended at the house. With the use of that exhibit, can you explain to the Court what happened inside that house, what you did and what you saw?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: I spoke to the woman. I had an interpreter with me at the time, and you can see the interpreter on the left-hand side of the picture. We went inside the house and she, the woman who you can see here in the picture, showed me her friend or relative, I am not aware of who he was, the man in the centre here, who was injured on the bed -- shall I say the sofa. This is the house, house 14, in question. This is the woman who beckoned me. And the man had received a gun-shot wound to the back, which I discovered when I removed a jersey -- sorry, removed his jersey up his back and saw an entrance and an exit wound, and what I believe the round had gone into his elbow, causing him basically two injuries from the same bullet. No dressings had been placed on him, and, therefore, I took out a field dressing, which you can see in the exhibit, and placed one on his elbow and one around his waist and his back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the man saying anything to the interpreter?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Not particularly. He was in a lot of pain. I can't remember him actually saying anything specifically, but he was in a lot of pain, moaning a lot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the clothing the man was wearing?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: He was wearing a jersey. You can see in the picture a diamond-patterned jersey.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the result of your first aid? What did you --

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Well, it was clear from -- that the injury -- he'd been bleeding, and they had not made much of attempt to stem the bleeding. And having looked at the sofa which was saturated with a lot of his blood, quite a lot, I would say he'd been there a few hours, also, which the nature of the blood, the darkness of a lot of the blood which had congealed, we, therefore, placed, first of all, a dressing on his elbow, and then put a dressing around his back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the general atmosphere in the house like at that time, what was the mood?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: One of shock and panic and fear. And in the back of the house there was another room where the majority of the family, mainly women, old ladies and some children, were hiding, and were quite clearly in shock and were very scared, and really didn't come out, but you can see in this picture a couple of the elder members of the family who had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And looking at the other exhibit, P79. Is it P79, if I can ask the usher? You're looking at P79. That further describes the scene; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. This is one of my soldiers, and as you can see we have a dressing around the waist of the injured man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what subsequently happened to the injured man? Was he taken away or did you leave him at --

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: We attempted to put a drip in him but failed. We couldn't get a vein, he was quite cold, having lost a lot of blood. And we were focusing too much on one incident, where I had not conducted a full clearance or reconnaissance of the village, and, therefore, having done probably as much as we could for him, I felt it necessary to push on up to the village to ensure our own safety rather than put ourselves in jeopardy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the expectation of you in relation to you attending the village -- in relation to you attending the village regarding the UNPROFOR base?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: The expectation or the task I was given was simply to observe and report on the conditions and the activities in the village, but it was only through, I suppose, a human conscience that we get involved in first-aid and probably took out focus off the overall task, which was just reporting the incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you drove up the village, is that correct, up the main road of the village?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you explain to the Court, using the exhibit, the aerial map, where in fact you went?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: From the first house, as I've already just mentioned, 14, we then drove up the village, which is generally a northerly direction along here, to this area, which was not actually there at the time, it was a lot narrower, and then along up the track heading roughly north-east to Point II where there's a fork in the track and a tarmac clearing where we could turn the vehicle, and that was the limit which I explored it to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that that was an area that is on the aerial photograph that is not -- was not in that state as it appears in the aerial photograph back in 1993. Is that that white patch in the middle of the aerial photograph?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: That's correct. That's now been bulldozed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of area was it, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: It was a similar sort of area, but it was just not as large. It was a small tarmaced area and it's now been increased by, I imagine, two or three times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you went up towards the location at the top of the village, location II, can you tell the Court whether your first impressions as to what you believed had occurred was still the same or had they changed by the time you got to the top of the village?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: My opinions weren't changing at that point, because I'd spoken to the Muslim lady in this Muslim village, and from what she told me and from what I saw myself, it was quite clear that there had been a Croat offensive in the early morning, about 6.00, and that there were many injured civilians, and some dead ones as well, and that's the only evidence I had of injured civilians and burning civilian houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from the route you took to the top of the village, can you explain to the Court the amount of damage, if any, that you saw within that village?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Houses were burning. Probably I'd say in the region of 20 per cent of the houses appeared to be burning -- or, sorry, were burning. It appeared to be about 20 per cent. And the road and the area was deserted to, my view anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In terms of that figure of 20 per cent, what was your field of view as you went up the road? Was it to the left and right, or was it further than --

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: It was mainly to the right, which is mainly to the north-east. There were a lot of houses that we can see on this aerial photograph which, to me, were then in dead ground. But from what I could see, there was probably a larger percentage of 20 per cent, but overall now, looking at aerial photograph, I would assess it to be about 20 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got to the top of the village, what did you do, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: I went to the top of the village to make sure that I had cleared this sort of whole area for my own safety and also in order that I could report back to my superiors and give a report on what I had seen. I deemed the Point II on the map of the exhibit that we can see as the necessary limit of what I had to move to. When I got -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me for one moment. Did you see any military activity as you attended to Point II at the top of the village?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: I saw no military activity up to Point II. Just smoking houses, burning houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see at Point II?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: At Point II, I stopped there for about ten minutes because our attention was caught by soldiers in the woodlands, which you can see here in this goose egg, to the north-east. The woodland at the time was -- in April, it was -- there was no foliage, and therefore it was quite easy to see five or six men, soldiers, who were dressed in green, with no distinctive badge, actually in the woods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to say from which military group those soldiers belonged to, despite the fact that you didn't see the badges on their sleeves?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I knew they were soldiers as they were carrying Kalashnikov rifles. I would say that -- I say that they are HVO soldiers, and this assumption was brought -- I concluded as a result of their position. They were looking into the village. The village is Muslim and they were on the periphery of the village and they were looking into it. It would seem that if you were a Muslim soldier, you would be looking out in order to defend the village, and their position was at the bottom of what I called a reverse slope, this slope where the wooded feature is here (indicating). So if the men were Muslim, they would either need to be closer into the village in order to defend it or need to be out, up on this high ground, in order to gain a good field of view in case any further aggression occurred from the Croats. However, if a Croat force had come through this village, clearing it, it could very easily have formed up at the edge of the village in order to observe prior to any further attack or to assess the damage that it actually had achieved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that it's on the record, the area which you identified as five soldiers which you have concluded were HVO soldiers, that's the area with the oval circle above the Point II?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: That's correct, this goose egg shape here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Everything that you saw that day or any significant events that you saw that day, did you record them in a diary?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I had a diary that I filled out every day, at the end of every day, throughout the whole of my tour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to producing a statement that was requested of you by the Tribunal and coming to court today, have you used that diary to refresh your memory as to what you saw?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in relation to your conclusion about the HVO soldiers being at the edge of the forest just above Point II, was that fact recorded in your diary?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: That was. On that day, it was recorded as HVO soldiers on that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that stage, were you aware of a War Crimes Tribunal in operation or going to be in operation?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were at Point II for about ten minutes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just to put the Court in some sort of time frame, you said you arrived at the village at 11.30. How long were you in the first house for when you were attending to the man with the gunshot wound?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Myself, probably between 30 and 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you drove to the top of the village. You were there for ten minutes?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You observed the HVO soldiers, and then did you go to another house?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: I did. On my way up to Point II, I had noticed on my right-hand side an elderly man beckoning me from his doorway into his house, but I ignored him because my task at the time was to ensure that the area was clear and that it was safe for my own men, and therefore, I carried on to Point II. But on my return, thinking my task done and that I had reported back what I had seen with regard the destruction of civilian houses and the one casualty we had seen so far, I then came across the man again who was beckoning, I submitted to, and jumped off my vehicle and entered his house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he explain to you, before you entered the house, what he wanted you to do?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: No, he didn't, no. But I could see from the distress on his face and his gesticulations that he was obviously in a state and that there was something very wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from seeing this man beckoning you into the house, was this the only person that you saw as you drove from Point I, down by the lower mosque, to Point II at the top of the village?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Yes, that I can recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at Prosecution Exhibit P222, I'll ask you what that, in fact, is an exhibit of, but can you explain to the Court what you saw inside the house and what you did?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: This is an area of the village where -- just short of the house which you would see off to the left of this breeze block building here, and this is one of my vehicles covering the route downwards for our own security, and this is an armoured ambulance which came some time after because, if I explain what happened, I went into the house that the man beckoned me into, and lying on a makeshift stretcher, makeshift out of clothes and two branches, was a person who was a casualty, a large person, elderly, which I initially believed to be a man, subsequently found to be a woman, who had --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: -- who had got an injury in the head. As I went into the house and dealt with this casualty, I took what was something like a towel, it was a towel, a tea towel, from around her head to find an exposed wound, a large wound at the top right rear of her head which did not have any skull remaining but really just had brain matter, blood and sinew and what I can only describe as brain matter, having never seen anything quite like this before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do in relation to that wound?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Sorry, yes. I took the dirty, saturated field dressing -- sorry, towel, off the women's head and replaced it with a fresh field dressing around her head. She was also suffering -- her breathing was very weak and very shallow and very slow, and therefore, we put a plastic airway to assist her breathing into her mouth, which was quite a struggle. She had one eye open, her right eye open, and her left eye was closed with a lot of bruising, which I think was peripheral to the main injury, and her jaw was very difficult to pry open in order to get this airway in. We also attempted to put a drip in her, but she was so cold and her veins were so -- well, they were not obvious, they were very further in her, that we couldn't get a drip in her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from the elderly man and the woman that you attended to, were there any other people inside that house?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Not inside that house -- sorry. There was the casualty, the woman, the man who was the husband, and then there was a few other older men and women in the house who were obviously distressed but were taking cover by remaining in the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would ask that you look at Exhibits 215, 216, and 221, and I believe these will describe the scene which you've just mentioned. Exhibit 215 first. Can you explain what you see in that photograph in relation to what you, in fact, did?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Okay. This is the woman on a makeshift stretcher. We can see here the private soldier with his hand over the airway to see whether she is breathing or not. You can see the fresh field dressing that I put around her head, and this is one of my corporals who is medically trained to a higher level than anybody else on the team.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is his name?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Lance Corporal Priestly. He was conducting the majority of the first aid, and here is another private soldier also in attendance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at Exhibit 221; can you explain what's happening in that scene?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: This is the elderly man had who beckoned me. This is me conducting some first aid. I think we were supporting her head or finishing off the tying of the field dressing. And this is the soldier, again, just attending generally, and this is my interpreter, and this is one of the other elderly occupants of the house, and we are trying to assist her in her situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at Exhibit 216, can you explain that scene, please?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: This is Ranger Farmer, the private soldier just assisting the woman, having gotten the plastic airway into her mouth and getting her breathing, and, she, as you see, conscious, although I would describe her as semiconscious, quite clearly badly injured, as I say, in the top right-hand part of her head from what I, with my limited experience, could identify as some kind of individual shot, a gunshot wound, and nothing else that I could imagine had caused this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you to look at two further photographs which are new exhibits, being marked 394 and 397. That's an internal marking.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The photographs are marked 230 and 231.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at Exhibit 231 in a moment, can you explain to the Court that scene?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Again, this is me here (indicating) just attending generally to the first aid of the woman having had the field dressing on her head. This is the soldier again assisting, and clearly the interpreter here was helping with the situation through his ability to interpret the language, and one of the relatives or friends in distress of the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the atmosphere in that house to the Court? What was the mood?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: The mood was shock, fear, panic. I think, really, "shock" sums it up in that the family, up and to that point, three hours ago, had their friend, their relative, going about her normal daily business and had then been shot in the head, putting her in the situation we see her now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I would ask that the usher produce Prosecution Exhibit 230.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you could explain that scene to the court? Sorry, 231.

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: When we had done as much as we could in the way of first aid in that we had dressed her head and put an airway in her and failed to get a drip in her, we then had called an ambulance from the UNPROFOR base at Vitez which had come up and we had seen in one of the earlier exhibits, an armoured ambulance, and we were now placing the woman from her makeshift stretcher onto a proper army stretcher that you can see here in order that we can evacuate her from the area of Ahmici to Travnik hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I'm afraid we must break now because we had a meeting at half past 12.00 with other Judges. We will resume at 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.35 p.m. 21 22 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. While we are waiting again for the witness, may I suggest that if the Prosecutor has some difficulty in handing in a list of witnesses for next week, they may probably prepare a list of those witnesses they intend to call, you intend to call; however, not in the right order, the order may be sorted out maybe on Monday, so that Defence counsel, in any case, know who is going to be called next week and they can prepare over the weekend. We discussed this matter at lunchtime and we thought that probably Defence counsel may wish to go back to their own country or, anyway, take some time off. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. During the lunch break, we have established a list of the witnesses. We will hand it over to Defence counsel this afternoon, but, of course, we may change the order of appearance of these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Welcome back, Major Woolley. I hope you had an enjoyable lunch.

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where we left off earlier, you visited the village of Ahmici, and you went to the house, the first house, where a man was shot, and then you stated that you went up to the end of the village and had a look around and saw what you thought to be HVO soldiers. Then you went down to another house, a house where there was a woman that was shot in her head. We started to go through a few photographs, and you were describing what the atmosphere was like in that particular house. At that second house that you went to, can you explain to the Court about how long you were there?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: I would say up to an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the result of that incident? After you had given her some first aid, what did you decide to do and what happened at that point?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Having given her first aid to our maximum ability, we then had her casuvacced, casualty evacuation, and we then gave a situation report of what we had conducted and then decided to withdraw from Ahmici back to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we move on from this house and understand the route that you took down further down the village and what happened to you after that, I would like to show you two further exhibits which haven't been tendered in evidence. The first one is a copy of a house with a vehicle in front of it which, in fact, Your Honours have copies, the black and white copies that were given previously, and the second one is of a destroyed house, and I would like you to have a look at them, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The photograph with the house, with the vehicle in front, will be Exhibit 232. You have a black and white copy of that one. And the other photograph, Exhibit 233, 2-3-3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can ask the usher to show you the Exhibit P232, the undestroyed house, and if you can explain to the Court what that picture is of?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: This is the house which we came across which, on our way up to the top of the village, had the man outside coaxing us to help him and who then we subsequently helped. It had a number 43 outside the doorway, and you can see of note is this Rayburn-type cooker and the breeze block building on its left-hand side, and here is one of our Warrior vehicles parked in front of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the assistance that you and your colleagues gave occurred just inside the front door of that house?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Yeah, just to the right as you go inside the front door. This is a photograph from the 16th of April.
