The flat trajectory of the ammunition going across the valley in that it wasn't like this but it was flat like that, shows that the rounds were of a high velocity, and they were being fired at a rate of fire where there were about up to, say, ten tracer element or rounds in the air at any one time, and this is consistent with an anti-aircraft gun. Tanks fire rounds one at a time. Machine-guns fire with a rapid rate of fire where you have a lot of rounds in the air of a much smaller nature. My training -- I'm a gunnery officers in the Royal Armoured Corps, and this is why I know about ballistics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me what the time was when you filmed the men carrying the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Which men carrying which weapons?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the photograph that was shown to you. One photograph shows people not wearing uniforms with automatic rifles, and I'm interested in knowing when that picture was taken.

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: That picture, if you're referring to the picture that has two men in brown jackets carrying AK-47s, that was taken at about 11.00, 11.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On their civilian clothing did they have any signs showing that they belonged to any army?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, according to the rules of the British army, would you do with individuals carrying firearms, without having any insignia as belonging to an army? Which category would you place those individuals in?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Depends how they are dressed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Like the people dressed that you took the photo of. If the British army were to meet men dressed like that in the operation zone, what would you think -- who did you think these men belonged to, what category?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: If that's a general question, if I came across --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am asking -- yes, tell us. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: If that's a general question, if I came across, in any war, men dressed in civilian clothing, with a rifle --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any war, yes.

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Yes. It depends which side they were on. If I could speak to them and establish they were on my side, I would take no action. If they were firing at me and they were wearing civilian clothing, I would shoot them. I don't really understand what you're trying to get at.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am trying to get at whether you would consider them to be soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: In this specific case I would regard them as soldiers because --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you in general terms. Generally speaking, if the British army were to encounter an adversary firing at them without military uniforms or military emblems, who would you consider them to be?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't know because they would have no emblems on them. The point is here, and what I think you're trying to say is these soldiers are or are not soldiers. Because these men are in Bosnia, and because Bosnia doesn't have a professional army with professionally trained soldiers, my experience is that you have any man with any weapon dressed in any clothing can be a soldier. So I don't see what you're trying to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I would like an answer. I'm not trying to say anything. I just would like to have an answer to the question, are they soldiers without uniforms with weapons, and without having any signs on their civilian clothes as showing that they belonged to an army of any kind? Would you not agree with me if I say that if they are civilians they would have to have emblems showing that they belonged to some army, or a five pointed star or something else. This is just an ad hoc, random example. Anywhere on their clothing.

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: If a man is wearing civilian clothing, he could be anything from a civilian to a soldier. This situation, whether it was the same for another British army situation somewhere else in the world, at the end of the day if you have somebody with a rifle, whatever they're wearing, then I would regard them by looking at the weapon and not looking at what they were wearing, and especially in Bosnia. What they were wearing was irrelevant, because I would say these two are soldiers is the point. I never doubted that they were soldiers. But what sort of soldiers they were, whether they were professional frontline soldiers or whether they were local defenders, I don't know. I don't know whether they were there in the morning or whether they'd come as a result of the engagement in the morning. The fact that they were standing there and they had no -- I had no -- I was not aware of them having taken part in any fighting, suggests to me that they probably came afterwards, unless they hid while their friends, and families, and old people and children were slaughtered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not asking you for your conclusions, I'm just asking you what you saw with your very eyes and heard with your very ears. What you conclude is your own conclusion, but in court it is customary for witnesses to set out the facts and then the Court decides on those facts. That is to say, whether it was so or not so. So let us keep to what you saw and heard.

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Before you asked me my opinion of what they were -- looked on as by the British army of any battle. Okay? So that's an opinion, isn't it. So if you want the facts, these two men were two men of combat age, they were wearing civilian clothing but were carrying rifles --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. And the part of my question -- I asked that part of my question because it belongs to your professional expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Let Mr. Smith speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I want to raise one point. I think there is a difficulty arising in this cross-examination, and the difficulty is I think there is confusion. The witness may well be confused from general questions to specific fact questions, and in the beginning my friend was asking questions of a general nature and only wanted to ask from a general point of view. This witness was trying to keep it in relation to what he saw and what he did, but my friend wants it had in a general way. Now the witness, when answering a question in a general way, that general question is being criticised by my friend for not relating it to the specific facts. So it's a mixture of concept and what he saw and what he heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Let me try and rephrase the question put by Counsel Radovic, with Counsel Radovic's permission. I think you -- probably the gist of your question was that you were keen to know from the witness whether under, you said, British rules, British military law, British rules, a civilian in civilian clothes, with no distinctive emblem but carrying weapons, would be regarded as a lawful combatant or as an unlawful combatant. I think this was probably the sense of this question.

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Okay. Generally speaking, an unlawful combatant if he's got no uniform or insignia, or is quite clearly not a soldier. But the point is, going back to specifics, is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So far this is the general question. I wonder whether --

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Can I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: That is precisely what I wanted to hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I wonder if you are interested now to take up the point taken by Mr. Smith, in classifying the actual behaviour of those two people.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: First of all, I wanted to hear that these were unlawful combatants because they did not have any insignia on their clothes showing that they belonged to an organised unit. And we stopped at that point, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Can I continue with that? I'd like to be more specific, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Yeah. I think we all know from the theatre of operations in Bosnia, whether the side is Serb -- or Bosnian, Serb, Croat or Muslim, the nature of how the war came about, you do have situations where men of combat age, and any age, in fact, can pick up weapons and become part of forces. Some are police forces, some are the army, but generally, if they have a weapon they are, in many cases that I was aware of, part of armies. They might not be on the frontline with a formed unit, but they might be part of a local defence, defending their families and children from being slaughtered by opposition. That's how I see it, and that's my experience of my time out there. Just because somebody didn't have a uniform on didn't mean he was a soldier defending something like a village, for example, Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, witness, are you an interested party in any way in this case?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: I am not an interested party in any way. Why do you ask that question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you this question because you go far beyond what you are asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I object to this line of questioning. Just a moment. This line of questioning is wholly unjustified, in my view. The witness was, first of all, asked his opinions by the Prosecution about military matters and he gave them. You, Mr. Radovic asked him his opinion and he gave it. Now you choose to allege that he's somehow an interested party. It may well be he's interested in the sense that he has reported what he saw that day, but apart from that, I do not see that he's an interested party and I regard it as an objectionable question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic, could you move on to another question, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as detonations are concerned, and shooting and similar sounds that are heard in a closed room, you mentioned that identification of a place that this sound may come from is affected by resonance, by echo. So my question would be: The identification of a place of explosion from a closed room, at what range is this? And also, to what extent does echo affect this adversely? That is to say this place that it came from, especially in an open space where there is an echo?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: That was absolutely clear. The --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm trying to put my questions clearly.

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Yes, it was very technically put. At the end of the day, when I was in the village of Ahmici, my experience of what was going on around me was obviously visual and audio, the audio. And what I heard while focusing on a problem like an injured woman, or girl or whatever, was noises in the background, whether automatic fire or the odd explosion in and around the area. And it was very difficult, while focusing on first-aid and what have you of these injured civilians, to quantify or to be specific about the nature of this battle noise, because, of course, you do have echoes, and I'm not being specific at all about any direction of any weapon noise or gunfire, and I'd rather leave it at that, because I can't be exact about it and it would be unfair to be saying anything other than it was just general background or peripheral noise explosions in a sporadic and occasional manner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't exactly put this question in relation to your own personal experience, but I really asked because of some other witnesses who said that they had identified where a sound had come from, although they were in a closed room. So I asked you because you were an expert in this field, and can you tell by an echo how far some sound came from? So I'm asking you this as an expert question rather than in view of your personal experience.

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Okay. I understand. What you do is you measure the distance between the crack of the rifle, or the gun or whatever is firing and the thump of the incoming round or bullet or whatever. The larger the gap between the crack and the thump suggests the farther the range of the weapon is away from you, and the shorter, obviously the opposite.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I would kindly ask you to look at this map and tell me -- you can look at the photograph behind you, the big one, but could the other -- Mr. Usher, could you please remove the other map that is on the big one? So this is the main road that leads from Vitez up to Zenica, et cetera, right? I'm interested in the following: To the best of your knowledge, do part of the houses of the village of Ahmici go across this road?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: I understand that -- I'm not sure whether the houses go to the south side of the road. I generally -- yeah, I think they do. The name of Ahmici is actually on the north side of the road on the map, and all my references have been really to a map -- my experience is from the map, and the problem with the houses in Bosnia is that you can have small groups of houses that don't even have a village name. So it would be speculation for me just to say now that the houses south of the road were Ahmici or that they weren't Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In your opinion as an officer who is a Major now, was this road of strategic importance for the HVO in case of an armed conflict with the Muslims, of strategic importance?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: This road runs basically east/west. And let me first say that any road is of importance for lines of communication and supply, but generally a road running east/west, from what I understood the situation to be, was not quite as relevant as a road running north/south, because generally your operations, the HVO operations, were south/north leading out of the Busovaca area and that linear sort of frontline running from Busovaca across to the west, south of this sort of area. So if I was a Croat wanting to advance, depending on what my objective was, I'd be going north, and, therefore, to have this road would be nice, but I wouldn't have thought necessarily essential, other than distributing logistics across my frontage to the east and to the west.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me, this road, doesn't it link Vitez and Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Correct. Yes. So there you go. You've answered the question. It is of some importance, because it's nice for the HVO headquarters in Vitez to have a little bit of a link with that of the bases in Busovaca. Very good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, if there were a group of HVO in Vitez and a group of HVO in Busovaca, is cutting off a line of communication between these two groups part of warfare strategy in any battle?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: It could be, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean, to separate these units and then to destroy each group separately; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: That is a very typical way of conducting operations. Yes, that could be done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you did not notice in Ahmici any significant presence of the BH army. What did you mean by that when you said that? That is to say, this should be elaborated in two directions. First of all, did you notice any presence of the BH army? And, if so, because you said you did not notice a significant presence, how was this presence that was there manifested?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: What I saw, as I said earlier, was no evidence -- there was no evidence of any formed Bosnian or Muslim army. There was no defences that I saw. There was no barbed wire, there was no trenches, there were no sangars, there were no houses which were fortified. The only thing I saw that I knew was Muslim and that resembled anything to do with fighting, were a few gentlemen in and around, as you see on this picture here, carrying Kalashnikov weapons. That's all I saw in the way of Muslim men of fighting age in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you base your conclusion on what you saw precisely that day, on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is to say that before that you did not come to the village of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: No. I drove past the village of Ahmici, but I saw from the main road, if you use that as a confrontation line, no defences at any point. Had I seen any defences or build-up of forces, I'm sure, anywhere along that frontline I would have noticed them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, when with your armoured vehicles you got into Ahmici, did you move exclusively along the road or did you go apart from the road? Did you go into the fields?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: No, I didn't, but what we did do when we advanced is we advanced and stopped occasionally, and using our times ten magnified sights did look into woodland in order to see any activity, because it's very important to look after ourselves. We didn't go off the road because you don't know whether there are any mines off the road. But as I say, therefore, we stuck to the road but stopped occasionally to scan the woods and the area for any threat to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me, when you were looking through the periscopes of your armoured vehicles, wasn't your ability to see what was around you limited after all? Couldn't you see much better if you would get out of the turret rather than only watch through the devices you had in the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: No, what you do generally when you're conducting reconnaissance is you use your eyes and, a great deal, your ears as well, and you look around and scan and look for movement, and then when you see anything that's of interest, you then use your times-ten magnification, your very powerful sights, which are far more powerful than any binoculars, and you pinpoint anything of concern. So "No" is the answer. Having said that, you know, my vehicle has a 360 capability, 360-degree capability. General awareness is far greater if you have your head out of the turret, however.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, on the basis of which facts did you conclude that there was danger of minefields?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: I didn't conclude that there was any danger, I was just being prudent because if you stick to tarmac, if you stick to tarmac, you have less chance of being blown up. I was not in any way trying to risk my life or that of my soldiers or my government's property, in fact; and therefore, we stuck to the tracks, as we do today and as I did when I was recently in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the part of Ahmici that is just by the road and part of Ahmici is on the other side of the road, after all, could you exactly identify every house that would be Muslim as opposed to houses that would be, for example, Croat?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: All I had was an understanding that, generally speaking, houses with four-sided roofs, pyramidal shaped were generally Muslim and that houses with Swiss-style two-sided roofs were generally Croat, and that was a good rule to go by. It wasn't necessarily 100 per cent, but it was a good way of adding to your confirmation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you do allow that there were exceptions?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Absolutely. But generally speaking, houses all around a minaret tend to be Muslim 'cause it's easy to get to your prayer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One thing that I'm not quite clear on in your conduct, when you went with your armoured vehicles and before you picked up the dead bodies, did you check previously whether there were any other wounded, or did you start picking up the dead bodies once you had asserted that there were no other casualties, wounded?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Referring to the specific task in the evening, at about 6.00, I was tasked just to assist Lieutenant Dooley and therefore we, rather than creeping in our mission, we just conducted the removal of those five bodies and then finished with that task and went back to our base in Vitez. So to answer the question, I didn't -- we didn't make a point of going into any more buildings to try and find people that were injured because that was not our task.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The dead bodies that you found, did you inspect each of them individually, or what did you do? Because you spoke of the possibility of wounding from one position or another, back wounds, and so on. For example, the body where you found that the wound came from, the entrance wound was from the back. Did it have an exit wound?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: I did not have the time to just -- because we were vulnerable, I did not have the time to inspect bodies. What I do remember of the bodies that were lying in the way I believe they fell, I -- on their front or on their back or whatever, they were not there as a result of being piled up or anything, they were there having either been running away, it was that there was several splotches of blood on those bodies in most cases which suggested to me that they had been engaged maybe with automatic fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I've understood that. But I'm not quite clear whether you looked for an exit wound or, if not -- let me ask this more exactly: How do you know that the back wound was an entrance wound?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: I don't remember talking about any back wound in this particular case. I talked about a back wound in the morning at Ahmici, which is the first man I spoke to. He had a back wound. The men that were dead -- sorry, the man in the morning, at 11.00 --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was wounded --

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: -- he was very alive, although very annoyed, and he had a back wound. The men that were dead lying -- the five men in the field, they had all sorts of injuries, and I didn't have the time to particularly inspect them because the entry wound seemed to have done significant damage and a back wound -- an exit wound seemed irrelevant, really, because they were not moving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Then we agree, with regard to the dead bodies, that you cannot say whether they were shot from the back or from the front.

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: No, but they were -- from what I could see, they were shot -- where they lay was where they had been shot or within yards of where they had been shot because they were lying in a way that was random; in other words, they might have been fleeing or whatever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, the opinion you have just given us belongs to the area of forensics, the mechanisms of the wound, but what I'm interested in is in what you saw with your own eyes, that is to say, whether they were entry/exit wounds and whether all the wounds were in the back. You said just now that you did not inspect the bodies and that quite possibly they could have been entry wounds, that is to say, from the front; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: They could have been any wounds. As I just said, I didn't have the time to inspect them. There were five civilian --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: -- lying in the field, and they were lying where they had been shot, and the fact is that there were dead men, some elderly, who were very dead. As a result of entry or exit wounds, it seemed irrelevant. I didn't have the time to look at them either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right, yes. Okay. That's all right. Tell me, do you know whether, on that day, there were dead Croats as well?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: I didn't see any dead Croats, so I had no need -- I have no understanding or belief that there were any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Believe it or not, it doesn't matter; the facts are what interests us. On the basis of what indices were you able to differentiate between dead Muslims and dead Croats?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: The houses. The dead people that we picked up were sitting next to houses that had been burnt out. You can make an assumption that maybe the houses were set fire to and they exited and were shot, but that aside, I didn't see that, so we can't presume that. But there were dead people next to houses in a Muslim village, the houses having been destroyed, the houses all very near a minaret, and these are the facts that led me to believe that these were Muslim people who were dead in a Muslim village next to a minaret and next to burned-out houses. These are facts. And also evidence from earlier in the morning where the woman had told me, you know, that she had witnessed an attack by Croats early that morning and that -- she was obviously Muslim, with her house, which is about 15 yards from a minaret, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But the people you found in the field that you mentioned, they were neither at home -- and the woman that you talked to couldn't have told you anything about them.

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: No. I agree, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means that, in fact, you are giving a conclusion whereas you have not got a concrete incident, and the conclusions are on the basis of what you heard from the Muslim woman and from the other stories, but no measures were taken for the identification of those individuals. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: That's right, no specific identification of them, but as I say, the series of facts which I've described led me to believe that these were Muslim --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all right. You've already told us that, yes. And now my final question -- perhaps I've already asked it, perhaps not -- but it has to do with the five men that were mentioned, at the beginning that you mentioned, that you met with Kalashnikovs at around 11.00 a.m. Did you in any way inform yourself of whether they were from Ahmici or whether they had come from outside Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: No. And as I said earlier, I wasn't sure where they had come from, I didn't speak to them, specifically those men, and if you remember, I did say I was surprised that they were still in one piece, having had no combat, because they were there in the village, and had they been there when the attack went in, they would have probably got involved in it so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Radovic. Mr. Smith, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Just a few questions, Your Honour. Re-examined by Mr. Smith:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major Woolley, I just have a few questions to clear up in relation to the questions that Mr. Radovic just asked you regarding the dead bodies that you picked up from the side of the road. You don't know the addresses -- you didn't know the addresses of where they, in fact, lived, did you?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's quite possible they could have lived in the area just next to where they were found?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my friend also asked you some questions in relation to the legitimacy of an operation such as Ahmici, and he mentioned the topic of -- the importance of routes as far as being legitimate military objectives in terms of securing them, and you agreed with that, that some routes can be legitimate military objectives and thus can be secured or can be secured within the meaning of the laws of war?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The villages of Loncari and Jelinak, how far off the main road are they, off the main route between Vitez and Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: They're quite a way off the Busovaca-Vitez route, but the route then bends round towards Zenica, obviously a Muslim area, and therefore I would say they're of less relevance to the Croats, to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can produce to you this map, it's a 1:50.000 map of the general area of Vitez and Busovaca, and you'll see the villages of Jelinak and Loncari, and can you relate that map to that main route --

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- between Vitez and Busovaca? Your Honour, that map has some markings on it which are quite irrelevant, so I would just ask that that be noted in the transcript, irrelevant to the particular point.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The map is marked 242.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at that map, can you point out the villages of Loncari and Jelinak?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: There is Loncari and here is Jelinak (indicating), and I understand -- let's have a look -- Busovaca I think is down this route, down here, this is the junction and this is the road that links Vitez -- sorry. This is the road that links Vitez and Busovaca down here, and, of course, here we have Ahmici. So this is the road that we've been looking at all day, and yet here is Loncari and here is Jelinak which, with regard this line of communication, are pretty irrelevant with regard picketing or securing of this route here. Is that the question you wanted answering?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be militarily necessary to cause the damage that you saw -- you've given evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Slokovic-Glumac? An objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, in relation to this part of the witness's testimony which keeps returning to the two villages, I must say that these events are outside the duration and time of the incrimination and the events of the HVO. These places are not mentioned in the indictment, and we hear for the first time that for this particular part on the 16th, that the indictment is being expanded to include these two places because they are not included in the indictment, we hear them for the first time, we don't know the time at which they are happening, and I think that this line of questioning should not be allowed because it outsteps the framework of the indictment. We also consider that we cannot reply to this because we hear of it for the first time as the region of HVO activity. They have not been put forward. This is the first time that this is being done. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The objection is overruled for the reasons I set out before when responding to the objection raised by Counsel Radovic. It is relevant, the facts relating to these two villages are relevant to the indictment to the extent that it relates to crimes against humanity and widespread practice. Widespread practice cannot last one day. It must, of course, last a few days or a few months or a few years. You may respond when it comes to the Defence case. In any case, we are now in the course of re-examination. So I would allow the Prosecutor to put his question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the HVO wanted to secure the route between Vitez and Busovaca, is it militarily necessary to cause the destruction, and in the particular case of Jelinak, the killing to secure that route?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: No. Jelinak is a long way away from that route. Jelinak is here (indicating), and this is the main route linking Vitez and Busovaca, and all that you would require to do to ensure the security of that route is push out up to the highest ground in order that you have a good field of view and field of fire, in order to picket that route as we've described, and therefore, Jelinak, I think, is far to far to the north, with several hills between it and the road, to be of any relevance, certainly with regard burnt bodies with limbs chopped off, et cetera, dead livestock and burnt-out civilian houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you ring the villages of Jelinak and Loncari on that exhibit? Thank you. Probably with a red --

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: Sorry. I beg your pardon. (Marks)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask that same question of you in relation to the village of Ahmici. Was it, in your opinion, militarily necessary to cause the damage and the killing that you saw right into the village of Ahmici and right up the road, in fact where you went, in order -- if that was an objective, in order to secure that route? Was that damage and that killing and that injury militarily necessary? Is there another way of doing it?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: It is absolutely unnecessary to destroy civilian houses, especially undefended ones that have no signs of fortification, should I say. Certainly not necessary to maim or injure or attempt to kill or kill children or old people, or livestock, for that matter. The way to do it is to basically close with and destroy any armed units that are in that village, take any prisoners of war; and any civilians or refugees who are causing a disturbance, to use a provost unit to secure them so that they don't interfere with the security of your operation and the lines of communication. I don't see any point in destroying a village and its people to conduct that intent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from those four men that you saw with rifles at the beginning of the village, were there any other obvious legitimate military targets within the village, like military installations, communications centre, anything that would tend to suggest that it was an obvious military target?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: In the village on the day of the 16th, I saw -- and subsequently anyway, I saw no dug-in positions, sangars, communication centres, any weapons. All I saw which gave me a feeling of anything military was four or five men at about 11.00 who were not in uniform and were carrying AK-47s.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if only for my own clarity, can you explain to the Court what a sangar is?

utterances.speaker: MATTHEW ROBERT WOOLLEY
utterances.text: A sangar is an Indian name for a defensive position which is built up from the ground with a series of stones or rocks or sandbags, a defensive post.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I assume there is no objection to the witness being released. Major Woolley, thank you so much for coming here to court to give evidence. You may now be released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Let me thank the Prosecution for kindly providing us with this list of witnesses. It is agreed that it is not in the proper order. You will sort out the order maybe on Monday so that Defence counsel will know how you will start. I wonder whether you have already included the witness, the lady that the Court is going to call? I had no time to check. So we will have to include -- it's not on the list. We will include -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it is not on the list, and another witness does not appear on the list, a gentleman who is waiting in the witness room. We had planned to hear him this afternoon, but I don't think it will be possible. It is rather late already. So I think we should add the name of this witness to the list, in fact his name should appear in the first place on the list of the witnesses to be heard Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: In the old list, No. 5. Actually, he has not requested any protective measures, so we can mention his name. No. 5?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I believe it is, yes, Your Honour. He has asked for protective measures, Your Honour. Although it is not mentioned on the list, he has asked for protective measures, so let us not mention his name. Yes, No. 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: He was scheduled for this afternoon, and then -- he will be the first one Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, he will be the first one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We will also add the name of the lady who should come over here probably on Tuesday, Wednesday, I don't know. We will make sure through the Unit for the Protection of Victims and Witnesses. All right. Thank you. I hope that soon we will receive the submissions, the Defence counsel submissions or suggestions concerning the visit to Ahmici if, of course, you are prepared and willing to submit those suggestions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Today? Wonderful. Thank you. So we will adjourn until next Monday at 9.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: 4.53 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 5th day of October, 1998, at 9.30 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
